card: Hegel spent the day in Cologne, looking at the Rhine and the many large two-masted vessels on it, and visiting several churches. For Sunday morning he planned to attend a mass with music in the cathedral, probably with the young Counts Stolberg and their longtime tutor, Dean Kellermann, and to leave for Aachen that afternoon.

Hegel reached Amsterdam shortly after noon and went directly to Dr. Besseling, to whom Mr. van Ghert had recommended him. Afterwards he visited the picture gallery, which holds paintings by Rembrandt measuring 15 to 20 feet across and 12 feet high. He did not get through the whole collection that day.

Hegel travelled on to Giessen, where he spent time with the philosophy professors of Giessen and Marburg and an associate professor of theology; the Giessen professor took them out for wine. Travellers bound for Frankfurt parted from the group there. Hegel and a Jewish schoolteacher continued together along the Lahn, passing Weilburg, a former princely residence.
Hegel arrived in Kassel at 11 in the morning and spent the rest of the morning and the afternoon walking about the town. In the evening he sat down to write his wife an account of the journey so far.

Hegel left Kassel by stagecoach on Saturday afternoon; the Englishman he had been travelling with stayed behind. Six passengers rode inside, three to a seat. Hegel sat facing backwards, opposite a student from Göttingen who held on to the rear seat marked number one throughout. The coach soon reached the river Lahn and followed it.

Hegel stayed mostly indoors in Koblenz, where Councillor Lange was absent, then on Wednesday afternoon took a boat to Neuwied and saw the Moravian Sisters' House. Next morning he boarded the Rhine passenger boat in rain, stopped at Linz to see a painting Schulze had recommended in a hilltop church, and at Bonn called on Windischmann and his son-in-law Walther.

In the evening, after writing to his wife, Hegel took the coach to Breda. There he viewed a tomb monument ascribed to Michelangelo, showing a count and his wife in alabaster lying on a black slab, while four standing figures, among them Julius Caesar, Hannibal and Regulus, support a second slab above them at the corners.

In Aachen Hegel sat in Charlemagne's coronation chair, shown by the sexton. He spent three hours in the morning and three in the afternoon viewing Bettendorf's painting collection, with Bettendorf himself present, then walked toward Burtscheid and took a sulphur bath. Leaving by coach early Tuesday, he reached Liège around five and stayed overnight with one fellow passenger.

With his luggage already sent off through a shipping firm, Hegel spent the evening of the emperor's name day at the Italian opera. Twenty-nine singers of the Italian company, among them Fodor, Dardanelli, David, Donzelli, Rubini and Lablache, sang the anthem in unison. Rain ruled out illuminations. The house was full, and a German cast premiered an Auber opera.

In the evening Hegel attended Mozart's Marriage of Figaro, performed by the Italian company: Lablache as Figaro, Fodor as Susanna, Dardanelli as the Countess and Donzelli as the Count. His seat was nearer the stage than on his first visit. The Kleins had extended their stay over Sunday to attend this performance.

Hegel spent 9 to 11 on a third visit to the Esterhazy gallery. Prince Esterhazy, told that a Berlin professor was there, had a valet show Hegel everything, including the private cabinet. Hegel then lunched at an inn with Professor Sonnleitner, director of the antiquities cabinet, and a professor from Padua. In the evening he saw Rossini's Corradino.

The spell of fair weather in Vienna ended. That morning the Kleins left the city; during their stay they and Hegel had done little sightseeing together but had met at meals. Hegel planned to remain a few more days to see places he had not yet visited.

Hegel spent two afternoon hours at the Belvedere, then saw Rossini's Barber of Seville with Lablache as Figaro, Fodor as Rosina, Ambrogi as Bartolo and the newcomer de Franco. The audience applauded entrances and passages, and kept clapping after scenes until singers returned. He read a theatre paper's notice on the company. The Partheys, at his urging, attended every performance.

Heavy rain began overnight and lasted through Sunday into the next morning. Hegel rested on Sunday morning; after lunch, despite the rain, he took a carriage to the Augarten and on to Nussdorf. Along the road he saw a large pear tree, its fruit already harvested, in blossom again, and he enclosed two of its blossoms in his letter.

The previous evening's programme had ended with the first act of a ballet in which the German dancer Eberle appeared. This morning Hegel went early to the imperial library to view works by Raphael and Marcantonio. Viennese collections were open free on fixed days, the library daily; he tipped the attendants at each visit. The weather cleared in the afternoon.

The day before, Hegel had travelled to Karlstein, an old castle with old paintings, about four hours away. In hot weather this morning he revisited churches and galleries, finishing his sightseeing. He lunched with the uncle's family, who then drove the party by carriage to a pleasure ground outside town. He was to dine with them again the next day.

Hegel arrived in Metz after 3 p.m. and stayed the night. He reserved a front coupé seat on the diligence to Paris. Before the meal he walked through the town, seeing the cathedral from outside and the Moselle valley from the ramparts. Afterwards he attended the theatre, where garrison officers filled most seats, for a play and a vaudeville.

Hegel and his companions drove to an abattoir and also saw the Bourse, Montmartre, which overlooks the city, and the palace of the Chamber of Deputies. At 5:30 p.m. he dined with Cousin and Fauriel, editor of the modern Greek folk songs. Some days earlier he had dined with Mignet, Thiers, Mustoxidis and Fauriel.

Hegel had attended a three-act ballet in Paris about a sleepwalker who is found asleep in a nobleman's bedroom and later seen crossing a roof with a lantern; only the first act was danced, the rest mimed. On the previous day he visited Saint-Cloud, on the Seine outside Paris.

At 10 a.m. Hegel drove with Raumer and his party to Saint-Denis, whose cathedral, burial place of the French kings, was still draped in black from a funeral service, and on to Montmorency. There he rode a donkey to the Hermitage, where Rousseau once lived, and climbed the heights above the town, with Paris and Montmartre in view.
Having left Paris, Hegel was in Brussels, staying at the house of his friend van Ghert. Madame van Ghert cut a quill pen for him, and he had a letter from his wife fetched from the post office.

Leaving Cousin in Brussels, Hegel took the diligence to Ghent on Friday morning and viewed the parts of the van Eyck altarpiece kept there. At 2 p.m. he boarded a horse-drawn canal barge, where passengers read or played whist in the cabin, and reached Bruges at 8 p.m.

After a day in Kassel with the Beers, Hegel took a hired coach to Marburg and briefly called on Suabedissen. In Wetzlar he spent an afternoon and evening with Schulz's family; next morning Schulz showed him the town and saw him onto the 10 a.m. mail coach. He reached Koblenz the previous day and took a bath before writing.

Hegel was going back to the Louvre gallery on its last open day before an exhibition of living painters, to meet Raumer and Panofka, whom he had met there the previous day; some days earlier he had walked through it with Cousin. At the Théâtre-Français he had seen Alzire, L'École des maris, and Emilia with Mlle Mars and Mlle Leverd.
